The school is proving that education rooted in community and land can nourish both body and spirit.
stories.extended_summary: When STAR School noticed students tossing unfamiliar vegetables, they didn't give up—they built greenhouses. In the high desert where the growing season is short, students now cultivate produce year-round, learning ancestral farming techniques alongside science. The program blends language revitalization, traditional recipes, and community partnerships, turning a lunchtime challenge into a movement that connects young Navajo to their roots and builds a healthier future for the entire Nation.

stories.title: Killing trees to save the forest: The deadly experiment to rescue the American elm
stories.summary: In a risky experiment, researchers are intentionally infecting 5,300 American elms with Dutch elm disease — to find the rare survivors. Those that resist the fungus could hold the key to restoring the species, which has been nearly wiped out by the pathogen. This project in Vermont is the most promising attempt yet to bring back the iconic tree.
stories.extended_summary: Gus Goodwin knelt in a Vermont forest, drilled a hole into a young American elm, and injected it with a deadly fungus. This wasn't vandalism — it was the most ambitious rescue mission ever attempted for the species. After more than a decade of nurture, nearly all 5,300 elms at this site will be intentionally infected with Dutch elm disease. The few that live could carry natural resistance, offering hope for restoring the tree that once defined American streets from coast to coast. It's a calculated gamble to save a species.

stories.extended_summary: 9-year-old Max Cortez races through wooden posts at Sister Cities Park, then stops to describe his dream invention: a giant RV with a bedroom, video games, and a garage. stories.summary: After Beirut's 2020 port blast destroyed public stairs, kids used Minecraft to redesign them. The Block by Block Foundation and U.N.-Habitat facilitated workshops where 45 children dreamed up slides, speaking-tube handrails, and seating areas. The actual renovations brought those digital ideas to life, and now the stairs are buzzing with life again.
stories.extended_summary: The 2020 port explosion shattered Beirut's beloved stairways, leaving them 'trashy and unlivable.' But 14-year-old Georges Zahar and 44 other kids didn't just accept the loss — they rebuilt them in Minecraft. In workshops led by the Block by Block Foundation and U.N.-Habitat, they designed slides and speaking-tube railings that became real blueprints. Today, the St. Nicolas stairs are packed with children playing on the slide Corine Abiramia dreamed up as a 14-year-old. A video game transformed a wounded city's infrastructure into a symbol of resilience.

stories.title: NC Budget Offers Rural Childcare Businesses Financial Help They’ve Sought for Years
stories.summary: North Carolina's new budget sends $97 million in federal funds to raise childcare subsidy rates, including a minimum rate that sends more money to rural providers. For businesses like Silver Bluff Kids in Haywood County, this is a lifeline after federal pandemic funds ran out, helping them keep staff and serve low-income families.
stories.extended_summary: Mary Moody's top-rated daycare, Silver Bluff Kids, had to cut retirement contributions and health benefits after pandemic funds dried up. But a new North Carolina budget just threw rural childcare providers a lifeline: $97 million in federal funds to raise subsidy rates, plus a 'rate floor' that ensures rural centers get more per child than before. For years, providers begged for this — rural areas collect fewer subsidy dollars per kid despite higher costs. This budget finally closes that gap, giving small-town childcare businesses a shot at long-term stability.

stories.title: Tackling the NC food deserts that Helene created
stories.summary: After Hurricane Helene destroyed Swannanoa's only grocery store, Bounty and Soul started a weekly produce market. Founder Ali Casparian, who experienced food insecurity herself, saw fresh produce going to waste at food banks and turned it into a free market. Now they serve the community every weekday across different locations.
stories.extended_summary: When Ali Casparian moved to Swannanoa after a traumatic experience, she faced food insecurity herself. Volunteering at food banks, she was disappointed to see mostly processed food—but also walls of fresh produce going to waste at MANNA Food Bank. So she started a small free farmers market. Today, Bounty and Soul runs community markets five days a week, serving areas like Swannanoa where the only grocery store was destroyed by Hurricane Helene. 'We had summer squash, tomatoes, and watermelon last week,' Casparian said, showing that fresh food is possible even in a food desert.

stories.title: Why Some Foundations Are Lending, Not Just Giving
stories.summary: Some foundations are pairing grants with loans and investments to help nonprofits build lasting financial stability. For example, the Bush Foundation gave clean-energy cooperative Cooperative Energy Futures a $2.5 million investment and a $1.6 million grant. This 'catalytic capital' helps organizations cover early costs that banks won't fund.
stories.extended_summary: Cooperative Energy Futures helps low-income Minnesotans access solar power, but it needs cash before it can qualify for bank loans. The Bush Foundation didn't just write a grant — it paired $2.5 million in investments with a $1.6 million grant, a strategy more foundations are using. This 'catalytic capital' covers staff, data systems, and early project costs, proving that lending (not just giving) can turn nonprofits into sustainable engines of change. It's a shift from funding this year's budget to building decades of impact.

stories.title: ‘Aunt Manda’s’ Ring of Dreams doubles in size from first show four years ago to 2026
stories.summary: The Wood County Fair's Ring of Dreams livestock show has doubled in size since 2023, now featuring 90 participants with developmental disabilities and 76 junior fair mentors. Creator Amanda Barndt keeps expanding the program with special touches, proving inclusion and community support can make a huge impact.
stories.extended_summary: In its fourth year, the Ring of Dreams show at the Wood County Fair has grown from 43 participants to 90, thanks to creator Amanda Barndt's relentless dedication. Participants with developmental disabilities get to show animals alongside junior fair mentors, with every detail from sign-up to show time designed to celebrate ability, not limitation. The Wood County Board of Developmental Disabilities and local sponsors back the event, which now includes Let Your Abilities Shine Day. This isn't just a livestock show—it's a movement of smiles, friendships, and real inclusion.
